threats.title: Server secrets or provider credentials are shipped inside the mobile app bundle or binary.
threats.mitigation: Provider tokens are exchanged and verified server-side and mobile only reads EXPO_PUBLIC_* configuration. A static check proves mobile source reads no server-only variable, and a bundle/binary scanner rejects credential-shaped strings and server-only variable names in built artifacts.
threats.residual: The static environment check runs in CI through pnpm test. The built-artifact scan runs against the release-candidate build (MTS-118); CI does not produce a mobile bundle on every run.

threats.title: Session or refresh tokens are read from device storage by other apps or from backups.
threats.mitigation: Session credentials live in OS secure storage behind a dedicated storage module, not in SQLite, plain files, or diagnostics.

threats.title: Evidence or Story working media becomes readable by unrelated apps through shared photo-library or external storage.
threats.mitigation: Review found working media written only to app-private document and cache directories, with no shared-library writes. The release-candidate suite must assert this and fail on any shared-storage write that is not an explicit user export.

threats.title: Diagnostics or logs leak tokens or private mission, evidence, or Story content.
threats.mitigation: Diagnostics are minimal with an opt-out, and a CI privacy gate rejects content-bearing or credential-bearing logging calls in implementation code.

threats.title: Queued offline mutations are replayed or duplicated after retries, reconnects, or multi-device use.
threats.mitigation: Every mutation carries an idempotency key and the server validates and applies mutations authoritatively, so replays return the recorded result instead of applying twice.

threats.title: A stolen or replayed refresh token gives long-lived access to an account.
threats.mitigation: Refresh tokens are stored only as hashes, rotated on every use, and reuse of a rotated token is detected and rejected as refresh_token_reuse.

threats.title: A forged or unverified Apple or Google identity proof signs an attacker into a victim account.
threats.mitigation: Provider proofs are cryptographically verified server-side; unknown signing keys and invalid signatures are rejected before any claim is trusted.

threats.title: A hijacked session deletes the account or its data.
threats.mitigation: Account deletion requires recent reauthentication with the identity provider.

threats.title: Credential stuffing, enumeration, cost abuse, or resource exhaustion against public and authenticated endpoints, because no runtime rate limiting exists yet.
threats.mitigation: MTS-110 declares a rate and body budget for every route, and tests prove no route is unclassified. Runtime enforcement of those budgets is delivered and calibrated by MTS-111.
threats.residual: Until MTS-111 lands the policy is declared, not enforced (see abuseControlEnforcement).

threats.title: Oversized or malformed request bodies exhaust API memory or parsing time.
threats.mitigation: Fastify's default body limit is the only ceiling for most routes and only media upload and feedback raise it explicitly (12 MiB). MTS-111 sets an explicit bound per route class and adds invalid-input fuzz tests.

threats.title: Server logs or audit records leak credentials or private content.
threats.mitigation: The API audit log records only request id, method, route label, status, duration, outcome, and error code, and the CI privacy gate rejects content-bearing logging.

threats.title: Missing security headers and no signing or encryption key rotation hooks.
threats.mitigation: MTS-111 adds security headers and rotation hooks for the token-signing, upload-signing, and token-encryption keys, which are single static values today.

threats.title: The cleanup job identity reaches storage or data beyond the working containers it must clean.
threats.mitigation: The cleanup identity is granted Blob Data Contributor only on individual working containers and is explicitly excluded from retained feedback.

threats.title: Cleanup deletes or retains the wrong media, leaving private content past its retention period.
threats.mitigation: Cleanup and reconciliation are covered by focused tests against real PostgreSQL and blob storage emulators.
threats.residual: End-to-end deletion guarantees are verified by MTS-114.

threats.title: One account reads or modifies another account's missions, evidence, or Story data through an identifier it should not reach.
threats.mitigation: Data stores scope rows by account and use composite account foreign keys, with cross-account isolation asserted in sync, settings, change-log, and media tests. The release-candidate and multi-device suites must re-verify isolation end to end across every route.

threats.title: Indefinitely retained feedback, screenshots, and optional email create privacy and legal exposure, including after account deletion.
threats.mitigation: Product specification requires a focused privacy and legal review before release. Retained feedback is unlinked from the account on deletion and restricted by role.

threats.title: Retried or duplicated requests apply an effect twice, such as double reward issuance.
threats.mitigation: Idempotency records and a transactional outbox make retries return the recorded result, and completion is authoritative and exactly-once per occurrence.

threats.title: Malicious, mislabeled, or oversized images are stored and later processed, for example decompression bombs or non-image payloads with an image content type.
threats.mitigation: Uploads currently validate the declared image content type and a 12 MiB body ceiling. MTS-111 adds magic-byte and dimension validation, and the rate budget for uploads is declared in the abuse-control policy.

threats.title: An attacker forges, tampers with, or replays an upload authorization to write media they should not.
threats.mitigation: Upload authorizations are HMAC-SHA256 signed, verified in constant time, bound to claims, and expire after a short time-to-live before any bytes are written.

threats.title: Managed identities hold broad storage access, so one compromised identity exposes every container.
threats.mitigation: Role assignments are scoped to individual containers, and retained feedback is readable only by a designated operations group with a read-only role.
threats.residual: MTS-111 adds explicit infrastructure role assertions.

threats.title: The transactional outbox delivers an event more than once or out of order.
threats.mitigation: Outbox delivery is idempotent and ordered per account through the change log and cursors.

threats.title: A poisoned or replayed Azure Storage Queue message stalls a consumer or triggers unauthorized work.
threats.mitigation: No Azure Storage Queue infrastructure or client exists today; the Azurite queue port is local development only.
threats.rationale: No queue infrastructure exists, so there is no attack surface. Any future queue must add threat entries for poison messages, replay, and role scope before it merges.

threats.title: Hostile text or images in AI Planner input, Story text, or imported event titles manipulate model output.
threats.mitigation: Provider output is treated as untrusted data: it is validated against strict schemas and rejected when invalid, never executed, and the user reviews and confirms drafts before anything is saved.
threats.residual: Prompt-injection cannot be fully prevented; impact is limited to a wrong draft the user must confirm.

threats.title: Repeated AI Story generation for one mission drains the provider budget.
threats.mitigation: Generation is capped at three requests per mission with the count enforced atomically in the database and recoverable across devices.
threats.residual: Overall request-rate abuse across missions is tracked under T-API-04.

threats.title: Stored Google Calendar tokens are read from the database or backups.
threats.mitigation: Provider tokens are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM using a random nonce per value and authenticated data.
threats.residual: The encryption key is a single static value until MTS-111 adds a rotation hook (T-API-07).

threats.title: The Google OAuth callback is forged or replayed to link an attacker's calendar to a victim account.
threats.mitigation: OAuth state is random, stored only as a hash, single-use, and expires after ten minutes.

threats.title: A spoofed Google webhook notification triggers unauthorized synchronization work.
threats.mitigation: Notifications must carry a channel token that is compared in constant time against the stored value, and the message number is validated before any work is scheduled.

threats.title: A captured valid webhook notification is replayed to cause repeated synchronization.
threats.mitigation: A notification is only a change signal that starts an idempotent sync, so replay costs work but cannot change data. MTS-111 adds explicit replay protection.
